clinical_knowledge.topic: Simple Finger Laceration evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Simple Finger Laceration is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Simple Finger Laceration, ruling out tendon or digital nerve injury, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: 31F presents with a 2cm clean-cut laceration on the palmar aspect of her left index finger that occurred while chopping vegetables 1 hour ago. Bleeding is controlled with direct pressure.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Simple Finger Laceration.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Flexor tendon laceration without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to bend the fingertip or reduced sensation — suggests tendon or nerve injury needing specialist referral.
management_principles: Evaluate distal sensation (two-point discrimination) and tendon function (flexor digitorum superficialis/profundus) to rule out tendon or digital nerve injury
Irrigate wound, administer local lidocaine, and suture
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.plan: Evaluate distal sensation (two-point discrimination) and tendon function (flexor digitorum superficialis/profundus) to rule out tendon or digital nerve injury. Irrigate the wound, administer local lidocaine, and suture. Check tetanus status. Refer to a specialty (hand surgery) team if tendon or nerve injury is found, and provide comprehensive wound-care counseling.

teaching.one_liner: A clean cut to the finger requiring assessment of tendon function and nerve sensation before simple wound closure — the exam, not the wound's appearance alone, rules out deeper structural injury.
red_flags: Inability to bend the fingertip or reduced sensation — suggests tendon or nerve injury needing specialist referral

must_ask.say: How did you cut it, and how long ago?
Is the bleeding controlled with pressure?
Can you feel normal touch on your fingertip?
Can you bend and straighten your finger normally?
When was your last tetanus shot?
